subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO DEVOTE THEM TO PATRIOTIC FUND.
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is advisable that unclaimed balances at present in the Chartered Banks of Canada should be transferred to the Treasurer of the Patriotic Fund to be used for the usual patriotic purposes.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in presenting this resolution to the consideration of the House

it is not my intention to go into any long argument in regard to the matter. I think the facts are pretty clear and I would just make a few observations in regard to what I am asking for in this resolution. In the first place I wish to be entirely frank with the House and to say that after considerable research I have been unable tto find 'any precedent for what I am asking in the resolution. In going through the law of the United States I find no enactment on unclaimed balances. I find that in the states of Connecticut, Idaho, Lonisi'ainia, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, New Mexico, and New York there are enactments on the statute books which provide for unclaimed balances inasmuch as advertisement is required of the names of those who are entitled to the money where money is concerned hut there is no final disposition of the money.
The law in all these states simply provides that the Government shall, in a public way, make these deposits known by advertisements published in the papers in metropolitan centres, or in Government blue-books, or in reports submitted to the Legislature after deposits have been in the banks for a certain length of time and no transaction has taken place in regard to them. I find that under the law of France no final disposition is made of unclaimed balances. In Great Britain, no ultimate disposition is made of these balances, although the matter has been brought up several times. The only precedent I am able to cite in regard to these balances is the law of the Commonwealth of Australia. According to the law of Australia of 1911 there is this statutory provision.
(1)	All moneys to the credit of a depositor's savings bank account (not being a deposit on behalf of a minor) which has 'not been operated upon, either by addition or withdrawal, for a period1 of seven years and upwards, shall be carried to an account to be called the depositors' unclaimed fund, and1 shall cease to bear interest.
(2)	The Governor may, on proof to his satisfaction that any person is entitled to any money which has been carried to the credit of the depositors' unclaimed fund, direct payment thereof to him, and his receipt shall be a good discharge to the bank.
(3)	A list of the amounts carried to the depositors' unclaimed fund and not claimed/ shall he published annually in the Gazette.
(4)	All moneys in respect of which a claim is not established within ten years after having been Included in any published list shall cease to be claimable, and shall become the absolute property of the bank, but the Governor may, with the consent of the treasurer, allow any claim after that period has expired, if he is satisfied that special reasons' exist for the allowance of the claim.
[Mr. Ross 1
This is the only provision I have been able to find which ultimately disposes of unclaimed balances, and according to the law of Australia as I have read it here an unclaimed balance at a certain stage becomes the absolute property of the bank.
For my own part I could not go that far. My resolution do is not go that far. I would not wish in any case to go to that length because I think the bank has no title to this money, particularly in this country where the chartered banks enjoy greater privileges and pay less for them than in any other country. However, I am not making this motion out of anything in the way of ill feeling to the banks, because I have none; I am making it from purely patriotic motives. At this time in the history of this Empire we are not following precedents. I cannot say that we are really making precedents, because the times are too exceptional. But, I think that on both sides of the House we are trying to legislate according to the special circumstances that we find surrounding us, in the best interests of the country and of the Empire; and I think this resolution, if adopted by the Government, will help in that great purpose for which we are all striving at the present time; will aid in the alleviation of the sufferings of our soldiers, and will help ultimately to win the war.
Most hon. gentlemen, I think, are acquainted with the existing law in Canada. It is contained in sections 114 and 115 of the Banking Act of 1913. I shall not read the sections, but, 'briefly, they provide that after, a period of five years has elapsed and no transaction has taken place or no interest has been paid on a balance in the bank, a report is made of that balance to the Government and that balance is published in the official reports of this Government. That balance is not taken by the Government except in one case: If a bank goes into liquidation ot becomes insolvent and there is money in the hands of the liquidator which is unclaimed, either dividends or deposits, that is paid to the Finance Minister and remains the property of the Government until some claim is made for it, and if a claim is established the amount is paid to the person establishing such claim. Apart from that, there is no payment of unclaimed balances in the way of dividends or drafts that have not been cashed, or certified cheques unpaid. By the law of 1913 a further amendment was made which renders it impossible for me to say exactly that the returns which we have furnished to us at the

present time exactly show the amounts of unclaimed balances, because by that amendment it is stated that any sum under five dollars that has been unclaimed for five years will not now be printed in the Government return. So that I cannot say that the figures I give and that I find in the reports of the Government are absolutely correct. I am not going into the old law in regard to unclaimed balances. As far as the Parliament of Canada is concerned, the law as it at present stands is practically the same as when it was first introduced in 1890. But I am going to deal with it just as it stands at the present time.
. There has been one precedent in this House which would jusify this resolution. When the Banking Act was being considered in 1913 by a special committee appointed far thait purpose, the hon. member for South Ontario introduced an amendment providing that all unclaimed balances would be turned over to the Finance Minister. That motion was put in the committee and it was defeated by a vote of fifteen to ten; so that I have this justification in the records of this House, that on that committee of twenty-five members, ten men at that time were in favour of turning the unclaimed balances in the banks over to the Government of this country. That is practically my motion to-day, except that I wish to have the money used fox a specific purpose.	-	*
There are only three factors in the resolution : In the first place, there is the question of the banks. Probably before I deal with that I should consider the amounts of these balances. According to the latest returns available to me, I find in the statement furnished to this House, of unclaimed balances in chartered banks in 1915, that there were in the banks of this country unclaimed balances of deposits amounting to $916,535.74 and of unpaid certified cheques, drafts or bills of exchange, $171,224, making a total of $1,087,759. I find also, on going back to the records of 1903 and taking the same items, that there were in the chartered banks of this country $517,272, so that in those twelve years these unclaimed balances had increased by $580,000. This question may be considered from three sides, and in the first place, from the standpoint of the banks. Are the banks going to be hurt by the Government implementing this resolution? The money is not theirs. According to these returns they have had the use of $500,000, half a million dollars of the people
of Canada, for twelve years, for which they have not paid a cent. They should be very thankful, I think, for that privilege, and -they should be willing at this time to give this money for a patriotic purpose. In the second place, the withdrawal of this money will not, because the amount is so infinitesimal, be detrimental to the banks concerned. I find on looking at this return that in 1915 the unclaimed balances-I am considering only deposits now, because the same argument applies to these as applies to other unclaimed balances-in the various banks were, in round figures, as follows: Bank of Montreal, $111,000; Quebec Bank, $15,000; Bank of Nova Scotia, $37,000; Bank of British North America, $73,000; Bank of Toronto, $4,000; Molsons Bank, $17,000; Banque Nationale, $19,000; Merchants Bank of Canada, $37,000; Banque Provmciale du Canada, $7,000; Union Bank of Canada, $89,000; Canadian Bank of Commerce, $103,000; Montreal City and District Savings Bank, $128,000. I shall not read the whole list, hut it will be observed that the three largest amounts are $111,000, Bank of Montreal; $103,000, Canadian Bank of Commerce, and $128,000, Montreal City and District Savings Bank. My argument is this: having regard to the large capitalization of these banks and the immense amount of their deposits, the payment by them to the secretary of the Patriotic Fund through the Finance Minister of the small amount of money suggested would not prejudice their business in any way. The deposits in the banks to-day amount to the enormous sum of $1,500,000,000, in round figures, having increased during the last three or four years to the extent of nearly half a billion dollars. At the present time, therefore, through the thrift and industry of the people, the Canadian banks are in a stronger position, so far as deposits are concerned, than they ever have been. Moreover. I do not (think they need this money- and this has been shown by recent financial operations. The Minister of Finance, with great foresight and great success, put on the market a patriotic loan only a short time ago. To this loan the banks subscribed an amount in the neighbourhood of $50,-000,000-I have not the exact figures, but they are familiar to the	minister. This shows that the banks were not very	hard up. If they	could
for patriotic reasons give to the Minister of Finance $50,000,000 on account of that war loan, surely they can allow $1,000,000 to go out of their coffers for the purposes men-

tioned in this resolution. I say, then, that the banks cannot complain if they be asked to do this. The money is not their own; they do not need it and the amount is so infinitesimal that it cannot possibly injure their financial operations.
If this resolution is accepted, the bill to be founded upon it will contain many details which could not possibly be set forth in the resolution. But if I had stated it to be my object to confiscate these unclaimed balances, what would that mean to the depositors? The amount of unclaimed deposits in the Bank of Montreal is $111,000, and in that amount 1,900 people are interested. Only three people are interested in deposits exceeding $3,000 and only fifteen other than the three are interested in amounts exceeding $1,000. The average deposit of the 1,900 people is $59, but if you subtract the larger deposits of the eighteen people mentioned, the average amount is only $40. The same conditions obtain in the Bank of Commerce; there are only eighteen depositors of unclaimed balances amounting to more than $1,000. So that even if it were my intention to confiscate this money, the amount taken from each depositor would be very small indeed.
In the third place, what are going to be the needs' of the Patriotic Fund? No one will take exception to the great work that has been done in connection with the Patriotic Fund; no greater work has been done in any country. If I have the figures correctly, there has been collected through the voluntary offerings of the people of Canada about $21,000,000, for the purpose of assisting the widows and dependents of the soldiers who have gone across the seas to fight the battles of Canada and of the world. I do not think that the people of any country have responded more liberally to these appeals than have the Canadian people. The people of Britain salute them for the generosity with which they have responded to every patriotic appeal that has been made. But there has been this criticism^and 1 think it is a fair criticism-that the Patriotic Fund has been raised by voluntary subscription and that at each successive appeal the same men have almost invariably subscribed. It has been suggested that when we send our soldiers across the water to fight our battles, the country should take care of their dependents by general taxation-and there seems to be some weight and some justice in that criticism. But there will come a time in the history of this war when we shall have 
350,000	or 400,000 men on the other side of the water. When the war is won, the patriotic fervor which moved the people to subscribe to the Patriotic Fund will not be as warm as it formerly was, and the people will not give so freely. There will be a certain amount of stagnation in trade; there will be a period of hard times and the need for some increase in the Patriotic Fund will be greater than it ever was. I submit that this $1,000,000 will be the splendid nucleus of a fund to provide for that day, which will surely come, when the people will not he as able or as willing to respond to appeals made on behalf of the Patriotic Fund as they have been in the past. On that account, if on no other, I think this resolution is justified.
There is just one more consideration, and that is the depositor. I am not asking the Government to take this money from the depositor. I am not asking them to do what has been done in Australia; I do not think that would be just and right. Since my entrance into this House I have been a constant champion of the depositor, and am to-day. I think that the depositor in the Canadian banks does not get his rights and does not get ample protection. He does not get his rights in the matter of security; he does not get a sufficiently high Tate of interest. There are many things that could be done for the depositor in the Canadian banks, and which will be done some day, I hope, in the near future. If this resolution is accepted by the Government and this money paid through the Finance Minister to the secretary of the Patriotic Fund, it will be my suggestion to the Minister of Finance that in case valid claims are made in the future upon the Government of Canada and those claims are established by proper evidence, these depositors do not have their money taken from them, but that this rich Dominion is generous and just enough to see that these depositors are paid the money that they have deposited in the banks of this-country. That is all I will say in regard to the resolution, and I hope I shall receive a sympathetic and generous response from the Minister of Finance.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO DEVOTE THEM TO PATRIOTIC FUND.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I accept, without reserve, the statement of my hon. friend as to the motives which have actuated him in bringing this resolution to the attention of the House. I think, however, that his patriotic feelings and sympathies

have got the better of his judgment, because what he proposes here is really an unwise course, and one calculated, if adopted, to affect our credit as a nation in which property rights are observed. My hon. friend has not carefully drafted his resolution. Just let us see what he asks this House to do. He asks the House to confiscate the unclaimed balances at present in the chartered banks of Canada and transfer them to the treasurer of the Patriotic Fund. My hon. friend does not state in this resolution whether the rights of the depositors against the banks are extinguished or not; he does not state whether the banks are to continue to be liable to the depositors whose deposits are to be transferred to the Canadian Patriotic Fund, or whether the banks are to be indemnified by the Government. I submit, with confidence, that, on these grounds alone, this resolution could not be adopted by this House.
Let us consider what these unclaimed balances are. The chartered banks of Canada receive deposits in the ordinary course of their business. Some of the balances in connection with these deposits remain unclaimed for a certain time and are then designated " unclaimed balances." At least I assume, that is what my hon. friend has in mind, because his resolution is so worded that it would really apply to all balances on deposit to-day with the chartered banks of Canada and unclaimed at this moment; but I assume that what my hon. friend means is unclaimed balances in the technical sense of the word, and I do not desire to take an objection on the score that my hon. friend refers to all balances, because I am aware that he does not. The legal position to-day is that the chartered banks of Canada owe those depositors the several amounts of money- comparatively small in most cases-to which my hon. friend 'has referred. Those balances are unclaimed, but they are not unclaimable. The bank is responsible to pay those balances when they are asked for by the parties entitled to them. My hon. friend proposes to confiscate the deposits. In one portion of his speech I understood him to say that, as the amounts were small, there was no valid objection to the Government transferring them to the Canadian Patriotic Fund. That would indicate to me that what my hon. friend has in mind is that those depositors would lose their rights against the banks. If they lost their rights against the banks, what you have
done is this: You have made each one of those depositors, who may apply for and claim his 'balance at any time, an involuntary contributor to the Canadian Patriotic Fund. The very essence and geniue of the Canadian Patriotic Fund is that it is constituted by voluntary contributions from the people of Canada. Yet my hon. friend proposes-if I understood him aright, and I am sure I did-to make all those depositors who have unclaimed balances in Canadian chartered banks, lose those unclaimed balances to the Canadian Patriotic Fund. I would submit that that is pure confiscation, absolutely unwarranted, and I am quite certain that the Canadian Patriotic Fund would not desire that those depositors should be made, against their will and without their knowledge, to give to the Canadian Patriotic Fund their unclaimed balances, which they may claim and have the right to claim at any time. My hon. friend would have been more fair if he had said that in his view the banks would remain liable to the depositors and, if necessary be indemnified by the Government but it is entirely unnecessary to take that course. If the Canadian Patriotic Fund at any time is in such need that public assistance is required, application will no doubt be made to the Government. It seems to me that it would be very much better that the Government should itself afford assistance, if assistance were indispensably necessary, and if it were no longer possible to maintain this fund by voluntary 'subscription, rather than that by legislative action of this Parliament we should confiscate moneys which belong to hundreds or thousands of individuals throughout this country and transfer these moneys to the Canadian Patriotic Fund.
It is a fact that those deposits in most cases are not called for and are not likely to be called for; but if any legislation is necessary in connection with this matter, it should not be of the (Jharacfer which my hon. friend has put forward, hut upon a revision of the Bank Act-and the matter was under consideration at the last revision- the question might be brought up as to whether the banks should continue beyond a certain time to hold unclaimed balances, as to whether they should not pay the amount into the Consolidated Revenue Fund to ibe available for the purposes of the Government, on the condition that the Government would indemnify the banks against any claims which might be made by the owners of the balances against the

banks. That has ibeen put forward on more than one occasion when the Bank Act has been under consideration, and that question would seem to me to be a proper subject for the consideration of Parliament. I know that opinions differ as to it, and I am not expressing my own view. The course which my hon. friend asks the House to pursue, namely, to' confiscate the unclaimed balances of those depositors without providing any means whereby they are to be indemnified-because the resolution does not anywhere refer to indemnification- appears to me to be legislation that would be regarded by the public, certainly by the financial world, as entirely unwarranted. It is therefore clear, at least it is quite clear to me, that the House could not pass the resolution in its present form.

speechtext:
I have not made a suggestion. I am pointing out that the resolution in its present form could not be accepted by the House. Let us now consider whether the House should determine to take these balances and transfer them to the Canadian Patriotic Fund, the banks remaining liable without indemnification or with indemnification. I think it would be most unfair to enact legislation under which these balances would be transferred to the Canadian Patriotic Fund or any other fund, the banks remaining liable to the parties to whom they are legally bound to pay these amounts upon demand; that wTould be manifestly unfair and unjust to the banks. What is the alternative? That we should transfer these unpaid balances to the Canadian Patriotic Fund, and that the Government should indemnify the owners of these unpaid, balances, the banks being relieved of their obligations. Now, that to me seems in no wise different from the 'Government assuming a liability towards the Canadian Patriotic Fund. In case of need, I am sure the Government would assist the Canadian Patriotic Fund, but I do not see the necessity for this roundabout course.
My hon. friend has pointed |out that while these unpaid balances amount to a considerable sum in the aggregate, it is only a comparatively small amount so far as each bank is concerned. I agree with my hon. friend in that, but I do submit that the principle of taking these amounts from the banks, who aTe legally bound to 
pay them, or from the depositors who have them lawfully on deposit, is unsound and should not be indorsed by this House.
My hon. friend has referred to the position of the Canadian chartered banks, and he is quite correct in saying that they are in a strong position. I do not put forward my argument on the condition of the banks, but on the ground that it is not proper legislation to confiscate money; I think that is the position that any Minister of Finance would be bound to take. My hon. friend has drawn attention to the fact that he has been unable to find any precedent except in the case of Australia, and that does not surprise me, as the course which he suggests is not one that would generally commend itself to legislators, especially under the British system. I did not catch what my hon. friend said in respect to unpaid balances in Australia, but it is my own view-and I am putting it forward only as my own view-that the only suggestion with regard to unpaid balances which would meet with the consideration of a legislative body is not that those balances should be transferred to any one or more funds, no matter how worthy they may be, but if there is to be a transfer it should be to the consolidated fund of the Government, the Government undertaking to indemnify the banks against any liability, and to make good to depositors these unclaimed balances should demand be made for them. Now, in my opinion, the time when a question of that kind should be considered is upon a revision of the Bank Act. I do not wish to be understood as in any way reflecting upon the propriety of my hon. friend bringing this matter up, because I know that he is actuated by the best of motives, but I do submit that even in so worthy a cause it is not wise to take a step which would seem to reflect upon the stability of bank deposits. I may say to my hon. friend that upon one or two occasions in the past when this matter was being discussed in the other House, I received inquiries from depositors, and lit has been brought to my attention that a good deal of anxiety was manifested, because the general public do not understand these proposals as we understand them in this House. In addition to the arguments which I have advanced, it is, in my' opinion, unwise to unsettle public opinion, especially at a time like this, in regard to so important a matter as deposits in our chartered banks. I am glad this matter has been brought up, because it has given me an

opportunity of presenting my views, and, such as they are, I submit them to the consideration of the House.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO DEVOTE THEM TO PATRIOTIC FUND.
speechtext:
It is not very often that the Minister of Finance is so technical as he has been this afternoon on the resolution of my hon. friend (Mr. Ross). The minister discussed the resolution as though it were a Bill presented to this House, when he must have known it was only a resolution affirming a principle. Why, it is not once in a hundred times that a resolution like this goes into details. The hon. member for Middlesex distinctly stated that he did not ask the House to confiscate this money, because when you confiscate money or property you are taking away something which belongs to other people, and appropriating it for the benefit of the state or some other institution. The hon. member for Middlesex distinctly stated that if this resolution were adopted by the House and a Bill founded upon it there ought to be a provision that if any uona fide claimants came forward and demanded their deposits from the banks the Government should step forward and make good the amount; in other words, the Government should gamble to that extent.
There is about $1,000,000 of unpaid balances in the different chartered banks of this country. I understand that an unclaimed balance must remain five years on the books of a bank before it is transferred to the " unclaimed balances " column. We know that the 'banks keep a record of interest bearing deposits, and another list of non-interest bearing deposits; the banks, recognizing the fact that some people do not claim their deposits, either through death or going away, and sometimes because the deposit is only a small amount, have made a practice of transferring unpaid balances after a period of five years, and there is now about $1,000,000 of these balances in our banks. My hon. friend from Middlesex now raises the question whetuer this amount should be considered as the property of the banks, or whether in these times of stress it should not be handed over to the Canadian Patriotic Fund. That is what my hon. friend asks for; he is not asking for anybody's property to be confiscated, because he expressly suggested that if any claimant came forward afterwards and established his claim the Government should make good the amount.
My hon. friend the Minister of Finance seemed to have great objections to confiscating property. But there have been many instance; in the last two or three
years where my hon. friend did not hesitate to confiscate other people's property. Only two or three months ago the Government confiscated the Ross rifle factory at Quebec without giving the owner five minutes' notice. They wanted the factory, and simply went in and took it. Nobody is finding much fault with them for that; they were only doing what they had a perfect light to do, but it was confiscating the property, nevertheless.
Sir THOMAS WjmITE: Why does the hon. gentleman say that we confiscated the Ross rifle factory? I understand that we expropriated it.

speechtext:
We will discuss that at a later stage. I happened to be in Quebec as visitor when the event took place, and, perhaps, I know a little more about it than other hon. gentlemen in the House. However, we	shall have an	opportunity of	discussing	that	at a	later	date.	TheMinister	of	Finance	thinks	that	_ thetransfer	of	these	balances	to	thePatriotic	Fund would	be a forced	contribution, whereas, he said, contributions to the Patriotic Fund were entirely voluntary. In many parts of Canada to-day that is not the case. When the Patriotic Fund was organized, it was on a voluntary basis but in many municipalities it was soon found that one class of the public were contributing largely and another class contributing nothing. In New Brunswick, and also, I think, in many other parts of Canada, the method has been adopted of assessing for the Patriotic Fund. And in New Brunswick in this way we have raised half a million dollars. We go beyond the ordinary assessment. An unfortunate policy has crept into our municipal, affairs in New Brunswick, and I presume in many other parts of Canada, of exempting certain properties from taxation. But so far as the Patriotic Fund is concerned these institutions and corporations are assessed. I cannot see any force in the objection raised by the minister because of the phraseology of the resolution. If this Parliament wishes to adopt the policy of taking these unclaimed balances out of the hands of the bank and giving them to the Patriotic Fund, the only question, it seems to me, is whether Parliament is willing to assume the responsibility of making good these balances to the extent that they may be afterwards properly claimed by the proper persons. I should like to see the money handed to the Patriotic Fund rather than left in the hands of the banks. Nearly
ninety per cent of the amounts will inevitably remain unclaimed, and sc the liability which the country would assume would be very light. I have no quarrel with the chartered banks; they are doing a good work and are in splendid financial condition. But I am sure the shareholders of these banks do not need this million dollars to help them to pay dividends, and I do not think it will be any harm to pay the money over to the Patriotic Fund, the country undertaking to refund any sums that may be claimed by bona fide owners. I am strongly in favour of the principle of the resolution and intend to vote for it.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO DEVOTE THEM TO PATRIOTIC FUND.
speechtext:
I have no hesitation whatever in giving to the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Ross) the fullest possible credit for bringing in this resolution, for Middlesex is a county that has been from the beginning of the war one of the most patriotic and generous in its gifts to the Patriotic Fund. At one itiime Middlesex led all the other counties of Ontario in the size of its contributions to the fund. So I know that this resolution arises from the best motives and is presented to the House with the highest purpose. But it has been the glory of the Patriotic Fund from the beginning that it represented the giving pi those who could not fight, and the slogan of the Patriotic Fund throughout Canada has been : "Fight or pay." The man Who shoulders his rifle and goes to the firing line is released from financial payment to the Fund, and rightly so; but the man who remains and goes on with his work as usual, who enjoys the privilege of staying at home, is asked to make sacrifices which, while they may not be commensurate, will represent something similar to those made by the man who is giving his foody and his life for our defence. To many people this is the only outlet they have. The man who is .over age, the man who is tied up toy business, the man whose home ties are such that he cannot leave, naturally welcomes the opportunity for selfsacrifice, and the Patriotic Fund has been welcomed by thousands and tens of thousands of our people because by contributing to it they are able to feel that they too are fighting the Huns. So, almost universally, the contributions have been voluntary. In the first year of the war eighty-five per cent of the contributions were not pnly voluntary but, so far as we were concerned, unsolicited. But it became necessary as the burden increased to distribute it. We found that the rural parts of the country

were not giving as much as the cities. By experiment we found that the people there were as ready and as willing to give as were the urban dwellers, but the difficulty lay, we were told, in making collections. When you have a scattered mral community, to secure a committee and have it solicit and collect contributions is a physical impossibility. Consequently, from the farmers came the request that they might use the machinery they had, the machinery of the county and township councils, through which the mpney might be raised in rural districts It was found that, generally speaking, the farm a man occupies represents his power of earning, and so hie relative power of giving. So we established the rule that where a municipal council unanimously made a grant, to he assessed upon the taxpayers, we would accept that. If there was a division of opinion, some members of the council wishing to give a larger amount and some a smaller amount, we said:	Give us the smaller
amount, but make it unanimous, because we wish to maintain the principle of voluntary giving So, while, to a certain extent the principle of taxation to help the Patriotic Fund has been introduced, it has been mainly as a matter of financing to facilitate the collection of moneys that people were glad to give. I think there are few instances on record in which money has been given to the Patriotic Fund through taxation in which the giving has not been by unanimous vote of the legislative body that had the right to give it. We have found, that, where grants were made by municipal councils with a certain timidity in the early part of the war, when we have gone back they have almost invariably increased the grants, tehowing, that they had taken the matter up with their constituents, and had found that more generous giving would meet wiith approval. So, I think that, from our Patriotic Fund point of view, there would be a certain taint if money were taken, you may say by force, from a class of people already generously doing their share. The hankers have been very generous in support of the Patriotic Fund, At the outset the Bank of Montreal gave 5100,000 payable in two equal annual instalments. Another great bank has been equally generous. From the rapid calculation I have made since this discussion began, I think I am safe in saying that the bankers have given annually $350,000 to the Patriotic Fund, and that if the war lasts three or four years they will

have given voluntarily the full million dollars represented by these unclaimed balances. "'So, speaking for the Patriotic Fund, while we have the highest appreciation of the act of the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Ross) and know it comes from the generous impulse of himself and those whom he represents, a generosity which they have again and again shown by their sympathetic attitude towards the Patriotic Fund, I do not think the motion should be passed if it has in view that the Patriotic Fund is to be the destination of the money. It is an evidence of the generosity of the people of Canada that though the Patriotic Fund is being drawn on for nearly a million dollars a month, and though we are taking care of between 50,000 and 60,000 families, so far each month has shown an amount coming in as large as that going out, and a little larger. The pledges given- for 1917, all of which will be available, I am confident-because the amount of uncolleot-able pledges in the Patriotic Fund has been remarkably small-are large enough to carry the fund through the present year. We hope to maintain, if we can, the feeling that the Patriotic Fund is money coming from the heart, money that expresses a sincere desire to make sacrifices, money given by people who want to do their bit; and we would like to have the Fund as free as possible from any feeling that it is made up of moneys taken by compulsion.

speechtext:
I believe the money is, or will be, needed for the Patriotic Fund. I have been active on behalf of the Patriotic Fund from the first, and I have found that the people who are giving year after year are the same people. If an increased allotment is made to a district these same people are giving an increased amount each year. We find hundreds and hundreds of shirkers throughout the whole of Canada, not only in my own province, hut everywhere, men of wealth, who are not giving a cent to the Patriotic Fund, the Red Cross, or any other organization. We have reached a stage where I believe we will have to resort to some other means, if the war continues, to raise a patriotic fund. I would like to see some means of reaching the people who are shirking. It is all right to get at the wealth of the country by the method of taxation adopted by the Minister of Finance but there are lots of people we are not getting at in that way who are making money out of the war and who are not contributing anything. As to the banks being generous, the banks have lots of money at the present time, any amount of it and they have a perfect right to he generous. They have great powers and great privileges given to them by this Parliament and they should give generously; more so perhaps than any other institution in the country. In my judgment, the banks have no right to these unclaimed balances. They would not suffer if they lost them. The president of the



Patriotic Fund does not seem to think that the fund is in need of the money but there are other patriotic causes that are in need of money, such as the Belgian Relief Fund, and if the Patriotic Fund does not want it why not offer it to the Belgian Relief Fund? These organizations are in need, the banks are not in need and if we decide to take this money away from them we have a perfect right to do so. I sometimes think that in this country we do not realize that we^are participating in a world war and that we can establish precedents and can do things that were never heard of before. I presume it is possible under the War Measures Aot to do a great many things that were never done before. It would be possible to take fifty per cent of the wealth of Canada if we wanted to use it to help the country at this time. There is nothing unusual in demanding at this particular time that this money should bp used by the country for patriotic purposes and to help in carrying on the war. I am in hearty sympathy with the resolution moved by my hon. friend from Middlesex.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not see how it would be possible for this House to accept the resolution as it is worded without doing a very great injustice to many people. The resolution asks the House to agree to turn over any unclaimed balances at present in the chartered banks to the Patriotic Fund. All that hon. gentlemen have said in regard to the worthiness of the Patriotic Fund I heartily endorse but it does seem to me to be a very drastic proposal that we should take any unclaimed balances, no matter how [DOT] long they had remained in the bank unclaimed, and turn these balances over to the Patriotic Fund. That, I believe to be a too drastic measure. But I do entirely agree with some of the statements made by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Buchanan). I do not see why the banks should have this money. It seems to me that we should decide on a certain length of time that these unclaimed balances would remain in the banks and that on the expiry of * that time these unclaimed balances would revert to the Dominion of Canada to be applied to the consolidated fund, the Government of Canada guaranteeing to indemnify the banks against any claims which subsequently might be put up. Why should this money stay in the banks, and why should they have the use of it for ten, twenty or

fifty years? It is not theirs any more than it is ours. It is not theirs as much as it is ours; I mean the people of Canada. I can see no reason why that money should remain there, and I repeat that these balances should be taken charge of by the Dominion Government, the Government guaranteeing the banks that they would indemnify them should any persons, in the years to come, make good their claims to these balances, and that under these circumstances they would hand the money back to the banks. But to leave them in the banks for an indefinite period I think is decidedly unfair, and I see no reason why it should be done.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO DEVOTE THEM TO PATRIOTIC FUND.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am in * accord with the views expressed by my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards). They are exactly in line with the remarks of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White). As representing one part of the county of Middlesex, I appreciate the tribute which has been paid by my hon. friend from Montreal (Sir Herbert Ames) to the patriotism of the people of that county. Referring to the matter of making a distinction between funds voluntarily sub-cribed and those produced by taxation for the patriotic fund, I think that our experience amongst our rural municipalities has been very similar to that in the province of New Brunswick as referred to by my hon. friend (Mr. Carvell). It is not convenient or easy to collect these amounts by subscription in the rural districts, and therefore the rural districts have resorted to a method of taxation. It is not money taken from the people unwillingly, because the people are glad to have an opportunity by this method of equitably and patriotically contributing to this fund. Referring to the use of moneys left in chartered banks, it seems manifestly unfair that the banks should be allowed the use of this money for an indefinite period simply because the money has not been claimed.
I do not know whether I fully understand the Banking Act, but from the remarks made to-day I take it to mean that when a bank balance becomes an unclaimed balance, that is after it has been on deposit without claim for five years, it ceases to bear interest. If that be so, it is manifestly unjust that the banks should be allowed to continue the use of this money. The proposal made by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) and the suggestion of the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White)

along the same lines would seem to overcome that unfairness of the banks taking interest which properly belonged to depositors; and if the money were transferred in that way to the consolidated fund of Canada and the Government thus guaranteed depositors who in the future would present claims, the Government would have the use of the money. In the larger number of eases, in reference to the great proportion of this fund, no doubt claims will never be made. But at the same time, if they ever should be made, the money turned over to the consolidated fund of Canada would be ample security for all depositors, so that no matter what turned up in the future the depositor who had in good faith left his money in the care and protection of a bank would have security for the amount, whatever it might be, even with accumulated interest.

Mt. ROiSS: And I believe it will be paid. But this demand for patriotic money is not going to end in 1917. No one in this House knows that better than the hon. member for -St. Antoine Division. I have heard it alleged in this House that there will be two ye-ans after the war before the troops will co-me back to Canada. Their dependents will have tp be taken care of during that time as fully and generously as in the past, and I repeat that I do not think the people will be as much up on the bit to contribute to the Patriotic Fund when the war is over as they are at present. That is all the more reason why this resolution, modified as has -been suggested by the Minister of Finance, should be passed. I cannot see any chance of the credit of this country being injured by the payment by the banks to the consolidated revenue fund of the small sum of $1,000,000. I do not think that the financiers of the world are ignorant enpugh of the stability and strength of our banks to be influenced by the passing of this resolution or of legislation founded upon it. Our banks are in too strong a position

at the present time for that. And, moreover, I aim not setting up this resolution as a precedent to be followed in the future. As the Finance Minister stated in this house on -another occasion, this war made a revolution of everything, the world is upside down, and things that might not be done in times of peace .are justifiable in times of war. speechtext:
Mr. ROBERT BICKERDIKE (Montreal,
St. Lawrence) moved:-
That, in the opinion of this House, and with a view to increasing the volunteer service and the prosecution of the war, the Government should permit all prisoners in, the jails, prisons and penitentiaries in the Dominion of Canada to enlist for active overseas service, thus enabling them to wipe out the stain of imprisonment and to fill up the depleted ranks of our boys in the trenches.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I feel sure that we have a great many prisoners in the penitentiaries, jails and prisons of Canada who should be given an opportunity to wipe out the stain of the disgrace of their being prisoners. It is a well known fact that voluntary recruiting for overseas service is pretty well exhausted, and that it is to-day costing Canada $2,000 for each man who volunteers for overseas service. I find no fault with that; I think the men are worth the money. I do feel, however, that these prisoners, instead of being shut up in iron

cages or kept at breaking limestone day m and day out should be given the opportunity to volunteer for service at the front. Some one has said: what would we do if these men deserted and ran away into the German lines? Well, I do not know that we would suffer very much in losing that kind of men.
I know of no other place in the world that has not instituted some prison reform different from what we have in Canada. The Government deals with this matter in a blundering, unscientific way, the basis of which is the stupid and savage idea of revenge-the idea that crime is to be restrained, if not prevented, by examples of punishment. Those who have made this problem a study very generally agree that punishment not only does not prevent or lessen crime, but tends, rather, to propagate it. This is so well understood to-day that the death penalty is no longer made a public exhibition because of its demoralizing effects. The harsh, cruel and revengeful manner with which our prisoners are treated will never in a slightest degree tend to reform them.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
I regret that I heard only a small
portion of the remarks of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bickerdike) in support of his motion. I notice that his proposal is:
That, in the opinion of this House, and with a view to increasing the volunteer service and the prosecution of the war, the Government should permit all prisoners in the jails, prisons and penitentiaries in the Dominion of Canada to enlist for active overseas service, thus enabling them to wipe out the stain of imprisonment and to fill up the depleted1 ranks of our boys in the trenches.
I confess that on a reading of the motion it seems hardly necessary that I should go into any very elaborate explanations of the reasons why I feel that the House should not accept it. So far in this war we have proceeded-we are proceeding, and we have it in contemplation to proceed- to recruit our ranks by a voluntary system. The hon. gentleman himself recognizes this, because the purpose to-f his motion is to increase the voluntary service by a system of voluntary enlistment. In response to the appeals made, the very flower of the youth of Canada have flocked to our banners and filled our regiments. The proposal of the hon. gentleman is that the Government of Canada should proceed indiscriminately to empty the peniten-taries and the prisons of Canada to turn the present inmates of those institutions
into the ranks of cur regiments. Prom the point of view of the soldier who has responded to the call of his country, and in the interest of those of our young men who have so readily and so willingly made the great sacrifice imposed upon them, I cannot recognize that it would be desirable that we should proceed to call upon our young men to receive into their ranks, as their daily associates, all of the occupants of our penitentiaries and prisons without distinction and without discrimination. It must strike everybody at first glance that there are certain classes of criminals who undoubtedly would exercise a corrupting influence among those surrounding them. I do not purpose going into details as to the nature of the offences to which I am now referring, but we all know that there are amongst the occupants of the penitentiaries and prisons, men who are there for offences which indicate the most degraded character, and still the hon. gentleman would include them with all the others and ask us to open the doors of the jails and the penitentiaries in order that those men might be let loose to associate, on a footing of equality, with the young men of the class to which I have already referred. So far as that class of prisoners is concerned, it seems to me that the proposition is manifestly unacceptable, and clearly calls for no answer other than a negative one.
In addition to that, there is the fact that crime in varying degrees calls for punishment, and I for one cannot agree to treat the enlistment in our army and the taking part in the defence of our country and of the great cause for which our boys are fighting, as a method of punishment to be handed out to criminals. For that reason again, I think the motion of the hon. gentleman is most highly objectionable and one that it is impossible to entertain. I do not desire to suggest that amongst all the inmates of the penitentiaries or the prisons there may not be individuals who might possibly be released for the purpose of allowing them to enlist, but what is proposed here is a general jail and penitentiary delivery absolutely without discrimination. That, I for one will not consent to. There have been instances in which the exercise of clemency with a view to enlistment has been recommended, and where that recommendation has been acted upon. There will, no doubt, in the future he similar instances and wherever the circumstances of a ease, in the judgment of those charged

with advising the Crown with regard to the release of prisoners and with regard to the exercise of clemency, justify such a course, we shall be glad in the future, as we have been in the past, to consider as a factor in ordering the release of a prisoner the readiness and the willingness of the individual asking for it, to redeem himself by offering his services to his country. Further than that, I feel convinced that we would not be justified in going. I feel absolutely convinced that the public opinion of the country would not uphold an action such as the hon. gentleman asks for; I feel the public would not uphold it in the interest of our soldiers themselves; or in the interest of the self respect of Canada and of Canadians. As I said, I have not had the advantage of hearing all that the hon. gentleman said in support of his motion, All that I did hear was a very general and very vigorous affirmation that our method of treating criminals was cruel- I have forgotten what the other adjectives applied to it were, but they were adjectives of a-similar kind. Of course, if the hon. gentleman considers confinement in a penitentiary a degree of punishment that amounts to cruelty, I must, on behalf of our system, plead guilty to the imputation of cruelty. If, however, the hon. gentleman means to say that there is in the administration of any of those institutions any undue infliction of cruelty, I venture to suggest	that he	should	oe readywith evidence to establish an accusation	of	that kind	before he
comes to throw it into this House and to cast it out to the public as an imputation upon all of the officers charged with the care, the supervision and the control of our punitive institutions. If the general statement is intended as any charge or accusation against those officers, I am in no position to meet any such vague assertion as that; but I may assure the hon. gentleman that those of us who are charged with the supervision of those institutions, in so far as they are under the control of this Government, are certainly not aware of any such state of affairs, and that we are careful in our endeavours to keep ourselves informed as to what goes on in those institutions.
I do not think, as I said at the outset, that it is necessary for me to proceed, at any length or with any greater elaboration, to offer reasons why this motion should not be accepted. I think I may safely leave it in
[Mr. Doherty.!
the judgment of this House, with the assurance that the House will be prepared to act upon the request which I make to it to reject the motion at the present time.
Right hon. Sir WILFRID LAURIER: Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the remarks of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, whilst I would agree in the main with everything he said, were perhaps more sweeping than they ought to be. I may say to my hon. friend (Mr. Bickerdike) that it would seem to me that his motion is certainly broader than he should have made it. There is a certain class of criminals who cannot be allowed to enlist and to be brought into the company of men of the character of those who have enlisted already and who are doing such splendid work; but my hon. friend (Mr. Doherty) will agree with me, I am sure, that there are, not in the penitentiaries but in the jails, many men, young men especially, who have been guilty more of indiscretions than of real offences, and that to those men the option might well be given of enlisting. Of course, they cannot be compelled and they should not be compelled to enlist, and I agree with what has been said by my hon. friend on that point. As to those who are confined in our penitentiaries, I am not sure but a similar discrimination might be made on behalf of a good many of them. My hon. friend said a moment ago that their crime must be punished, and I agree with him on that point, but there ari' degrees of punishment.
Years ago we introduced the system of ticket-of-leave, which I think has worked admirably. Under this system, men who have been found guilty of serious offences but who are not criminal by nature, who have been driven to crime, perhaps, by their environment or associates, and who have some redeeming qualities, are given their freedom before their sentence expires, and I am sure it must be the same to-day as it was under the previous Government, that many and many of the men so released turn out to be very good citizens. Ticket-of-leave, of course, is granted only upon certain conditions which ordinarily would not be deviated from, but I think the Minister of Justice might well consider the advisability of giving this class of offenders the opportunity of leading a better life by serving in the forces, and certainly they could not do better than to offer their services to their country. If my hon. friend will not accept the present motion, he might at least take the matter into con-

sideration with a view to arriving at some method which would be in the best interests of all concerned.
Mr. Turriff rose to speak.
At six o'clock the House took recess

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) I think, is not quite so conversant with the facts as some of us on this side are. Unfortunately, or fortunately, the hon. gentleman has no sons, grandsons, or nephews, in France. That is not his fault; I am not blaming him. But I speak feelingly on this question, as I have a son, two grandsons and seven nephews at the front-that is, I had seven nephews at the front, but two have been killed and two badly wounded. I do not think that anyone who has those near and dear to him at the front would object if some of the prisoners were in the fight and helping to save the lives of our boys. No such person would raise the question whether those men had been in prison or not. Of course, if is a disgrace to be in prison. But there are many in prison who perhaps should not
be there. And I am quite safe in saying that there are a good many who are not in prison who should be there. A good many young men are in prison for the first time, some of them for comparatively slight offences. I think these men might be given an opportunity to wipe out the stain of their imprisonment, and at the same time fight for the honour of Canada. I do not think the mothers of the boys in the trenches would find much fault if a regiment or two of our prisoners were helping to save the lives of their sons over there. They would not think much about the dignity of Canada if their boys' lives were being saved. I knew that the Minister of Justice would have an excuse-he always has when I have a resolution to propose. I did not know just what the excuse would be in this case, but I know it now-the dignity of the country, and the wish to punish these fellows. I admit that they deserve punishment. But there is such a thing as being too revengeful, and, while I do not wish to be personal with the hon. gentleman, whom I have known since he was a boy, I will say that I have known very few of his countrymen, the Irish, but have good hearts and have no wish to punish everybody, including the poor criminal-to shut him up in an iron cage, to throw him into a stone-walled yard and make him break stones all his life. The hon. gentleman states that there is no justification for what I said with regard to the management of the penitentiaries. What I said was not nearly so strong as the reports of his own Royal Commission. I believe he has modified conditions to a certain extent, but not sufficiently even yet. I hope the hon. gentleman will accept the resolution, with modifications if he likes. For, of course, I do not say that every prisoner should be allowed to leave the penitentiary and enlist; I speak only of the better class of prisoners, the boys who are in gaol for the first time, and, it may be, for comparatively trifling offences. I have in mind the case of a man whom I know, who is in penitentiary for two years. He got drunk and stole a horse and buggy, and was condemned. But that man is no criminal; I would not be ashamed to have him fighting side by side with my own son. I do not know that there is anything more I can say. I do not seem to be able to touch the minister's heart. I have been trying it for four years, but unsuccessfully. I pleaded with him, whether he accept the resolution or not, to do all he can in the way of helping to save our boys at the front.
Motion negatived.

speakeroldname: Mr. ROBERT BICKERDIKE (Montreal, St. Lawrence) moved:
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
-
That, in the opinion of this House, in consideration of the fact that the Russian Government has just recently abolished capital punishment, and that the population of this Dominion of Canada are at the present time much exercised as to the advisability of discontinuing the extreme penalty of death in Canada, at its next general election, the voters of Canada be afforded an opportunity by means of a plebiscite of declaring for or against such continuance of capital punishment in this Dominion.
He said: It is a well known fact that Russia has recently abolished capital punishment. I think this action was taken about the last week of February. Capital punishment has been abolished by many others of the Allies of Great Britain. I have no doubt-and possibly the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) will agree with me this time-that there has been a considerable agitation, during the last three or four months at least, on the question whether the people of this country should have an opportunity to declare whether 5r not they are still in favour of capital punishment. I think that in every province except Ontario and Quebec the people have virtually come out in favour of abolishing the death penalty.
I would like to place on record for the benefit of the House of Commons and of the country in general the final disposition of the twenty murderers who were condemned to death in 1916. Let me take off my hat to New Brunswick as she was the only province that did not have a murder committed in the year 1916; I suppose, largely due to the close proximity of the State of Maine. My information is to the effect that a large majority of the inhabitants of that enlightened province are in favour of prison reform and opposed to capital punishment. Prince Edward Island had one murder committed, the criminal being sentenced to death but as the people of Prince Edward Island are in favour of prison reform and opposed to capital punishment strong recommendations were made in this case against the execution of the sentence and it was commuted to life imprisonment which my hon. friend the Minister of Justice will remember.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: We are not so hard hearted as you say.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
Well, I am not
through with you yet. Ontario, nnfortun-

ately, looms up worse than any other province. They had four murders in Ontario, and as Ontario up to the present time happens to be in favour of capital punishment and against prison reform, all four prisoners were sent into eternity, three of them by the scaffold and one of his own accord, he having committed suicide. As there is now an agitation going on in different parts of the country for the purpose of abolishing legalized murder, I have hopes for that province in the future. We only had one murder in the province of Quebec, at St. Johns, and it being a very brutal case and the population not being quite clear yet on the question of capital punishment, the man was hanged. The Yukon had one murder and the murderer got the extreme penalty. I have no information as to how the inhabitants of the Yukon regard the death penalty. British Columbia, although a mining country, had only two murders; one sentence was executed and the other commuted to imprisonment. As far as I can learn the people of British Columbia are now in favour of the life sentence in preference to the death sentence and they are very strongly in favour of prison reform. Saskatchewan had two murders; one of the sentences was commuted and the other executed. My information is that a large portion of the population of Saskatchewan still hold out for capital punishment but there is a strong agitation for abolition and prison reform. Alberta was not quite so fortunate; they had three cases of murder. Two of the sentences were commuted and one of the criminals paid the extreme penalty. The people of Alberta are strongly in favour of prison reform and of abolishing the death penalty as members from that province will ascertain at the next general election because when they go back they ydll be asked whether they are in favour of capital punishment, whether they are baby killers, or whether they intend to vote and work in favour of prison reform.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext: It all depends on what you call a baby. A person 17 years old is not a baby.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
The hon. member
for Selkirk (Mr. Bradibury) would like to out-Herod Herod himself; he had better just wait. Manitoba also had three murder oases. One of the sentences was commuted and two were executed. Manitoba, I am pleased to say, is seriously contemplating requesting the Government to abolish capital punishment and is also in favour of

prison leform. Nova Scotia was not so fortunate. It had three murder cases and the murderers were all condemned to death by the courts, but as >the people of Nova Scotia are largely in favour of prison reform and the abolition of capital punishment, strong representations, were made for mercy and the three sentences were commuted -to life imprisonment. When the news was received by the population of Nova Scotia that they had succeeded in saving the lives of these three prodigals and that their souls were not sent into eternity, a sigh of relief went up, and I hope and believe that many of the people of that province before retiring that evening went down on their knees and thanked God -that these prodigals were sent to the penitentiary instead of into eternity. Any member of this House would be a bold man who would stand up in his place and declare that the province of Nova Beotia had suffered for that clemency and mercy or [DOT]that society had been prejudiced in any way by sending these three men to the penitentiary instead of sending them into eternity. I hope the Minister of Justice will agree -to this resolution at least.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. gentleman ('Mr. Bickerdike) expresses the hope that I may agree with him on this motion, I may say that one of my fondest hopes is tha-t the day will some time arrive when I shall find my.self in agreement with the hpn. gentleman on some proposal that he may make. He says that he has been four years trying to persuade me that the law of *this country providing capital punishment for the gravest offence should be altered and he describes my position as being one of hard heartedness. I do not know but that perhaps I might claim that my action was due to just level headedness. However that may be, I do not purpose to enter upon any argument on the general question of the desirability of the abolition of capital punishment and my hon. friend has not done so in supporting his motion. His proposal is that the question should be submitted to a plebiscite at the next general election. .As a general proposition, it does not seem to me desirable that we should depart from what is after all our system of parliamentary government and say, without some very exceptional reason, that we should submit to the people directly the exercise of the legislative power which constitutionally is properly exercised by their representatives in Parliament. I confess tha* I am
not in a position to know what the gentleman's sources of information are as to the prevailing public opinion in the different provinces as to the desirability of abolishing capital punishment. But, I may say for myself, that I have not had occasion to see any evidence that the public of Canada generally were so keenly alive to the necessity of any change in the existing system of punishment as to make of this question of capital punishment a subject which should be treated as exceptional and withdrawn from the control of Parliament to be committed directly to the decision of the people. I do have in my official capacity certain opportunities of appreciating what are the matters in regard to which the people of Canada feel that there is need for modification in our criminal law. I am in receipt of numerous -communications making representations in regard to one disposition or another in the criminal law and suggesting, and in many instances even pressing for, modifications of the dispositions there referred to. If my memory is correct, and I think it is, I have not had anything approaching widespread representations that there exists a conviction on the part of the people of Canada, or a desire on their part, that the law as it now stands on that subject should be modified. Indeed it would be difficult for me to mention any particular representation made to me upon that subject. Under those circumstances I certainly cannot share the view of the hon. gentleman that there is any such general unrest among the public uppn that question as to make it incumbent upon us or to make it desirable that we should take this extraordinary method of dealing with this particular -subject for legislation, of calling upon the people themselves to deal with it direct. For this reaspn I regret that once more I find myself in the unfortunate position of not being able to agree with the hon. member and to ae-cept his proposition.
Motion negatived.

That, in the opinion of this House, as there now lies within this Dominion a young lad of sixteen years under the condemnation of death whose father is at the present moment fighting with his regiment in the British Army in France in defence of the Empire, it is the sense of this Parliament that the infliction of the death penalty is contrary to the dictates of civilization and Christianity, and we hereby protest against the proposed hanging of this young boy of the tender age of sixteen years, which we consider would be a blot on the fair name of Canada and an everlasting disgrace to this young nation.

speechtext: Then I should like to make a few remarks with regard to it. It is really my opinion that the best interest of this young nation would be served by amending the criminal code as here suggested, more especially as this little boy in Manitoba has been sentenced to death, the sentence to be carried out on the 15th of May. I think my friend will agree that he has been approached on that question. maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
