speechtext: There have been representations made, but there is no such a petition as that.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.
subtopic: ABOLITION OF CAPITAL PUNISHMENT -THE SPAIN CASE.
speechtext:
While the House is not unanimous in respect to the abolition of the death penalty in its entirety at the present time, I do hope that the members will see their way clear to vote this resolution unanimously, so that we may be able to prove to the world that there are no baby killer members of this House, or at least very few.
[The Speaker.]
In an ever increasing number the different states of the Union in the neighbouring republic have abolished capital punishment. It is, in Canada, strongly argued that an individual indicted for a capital offence is tried by jury and has all the advantages of criminal procedure to make out his case. On the face of it this is true; but in the last analysis the person's life depends upon the good judgment, or the bad judgment, as the case may be, of one man only, the Minister of Justice. If the prisoner is too poor to secure witnesses, or too much of a stranger to have testifying friends, he is found guilty; but if he has the means to pay lawyers, or has friends to do so for him, he can have his case appealed to the Governor General in Council. That means simply to the Minister of Justice for the time being. It is on the recommendation of that same minister that the commutation or the allowing of the law to take its course depends. Scores of men have been hanged because they either had no means to push their cases to this last point, or else they were strangers in the land and had no friends to interest themselves for them. Herein lies a grave danger-a danger that would be obviated were there no capital punishment, but merely perpetual imprisonment. It is needless to dwell further on this phase of the issue.
It is in the interest of justice, in the interest of legal certainty, in the interest of the stranger, the poor man, the friendless one, the workman, the individual whose lines are not cast in the higher strata of our social life; in the interest of humanity and of civilization, that this remaining blot be removed from the face of our otherwise matchless system of law and government. Instead of being a step backwards it becomes a giant stride ahead in the direction of the higher civilization and a broader Christianity. When this terrible war will have ended and peace will again spread her wings over our fair Dominion, we want to be more in accord with the teachings of the Prince of Peace on earth.
' Let those who care to look into the problem deeper	visit	the Cotede	Neiges	Cemetery at	Montreal.
It was afterwards discovered that a mistake had been made and that they should not have been hanged. A similar mistake was made in Toronto when Lount and Matthews were hanged. There is no question about the fact that they were rebels, but they were misled. If all the Tebels in Canada were hanged, we would not have as

large a population as we have to-day. The lives of these young men should have been spared; the Minister of Justice and the member for Rouville will not dare controvert that. The lives of the 18 or 19 men who were hanged in 1838 should have been spared, and if I had been alive I would have done all I could to save them. Were their lives worth saving? I submit that they were, and I stand or fall by that assertion.
I may not win in this fight, but I shall at least be consoled with the thought that the blood of these poor unfortunate women and children would not be on my hands if it were in my power to stop it. It seems a pity to me that presumably good men construe the Scriptures in such a way as to come to the conclusion that the state is justified in taking human life. The horribleness of the thing itself is enough to condemn it, regardless of the doctrine of the law' of mercy and love as taught by the Master. Now I come to the boy to whose case reference has been made. Some one said that he was an Italian, and the member for Selkirk claims that all these murders are committed by English boys. The right hon. leader of the Opposition says that' many of them are committed by Italians. Well, if I were to judge by this young man's name, he is neither Italian nor English. His name is Patrick Spain; most people would think that he vras Irish. However, it makes no difference whether he is black or white, orange or green; let us remember that he is some mother's boy. This young lad when 14 years of age became a bugler in the army. When his comrades in the trenches come back, if they ever do, they will ask the Minister of Justice: what has become of our little bugler comrade? It is no use saying that you are not the bugler's keeper or your brother's keeper. That reply was unsatisfactory 6,000 years ago, and it will not suit when the boys come back from the front.
The question as to whether the world is growing better or worse has nothing to do with the awfulness of hanging a woman or child. The child is some mother's boy. He has sinned, that is true; yet to hang him is only doing the worst thing the State can do to him. The crime cannot be undone by taking the offender's life; nothing that society can do can heal the wounds of the injured one. Where, then, is the common sense in making other wounds, in bringing double disgrace on the parents, brothers
and sisters of the offender? Any man who reads the New Testament knows that it says:	"For whosoever shall keep the
whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty in all." How such a man can feel that he is justified in sitting in judgment and casting the first stone, is beyond my understanding. " There is one lawgiver, who is able to save and destroy; who art thou that judgest another?" Surely we are too enlightened to feel, as did the Pharisee of old: " God, I thank Thee that I am not as other men." Does not the Scripture say: " Let not him which eateth not, judge him that eateth." " Love worketh not ill to his neighbour; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law." " If we love one another, God dwelleth in us." " He that loveth not his brother whom he has seen, how can he love God, whom he hath not seen?"
If I am wrong in my fight to save this boy, then it is wrong to be merciful. If my fight to save the criminal's life is wrong, then the law of love is wrong.
There is another reason, almost fundamental, why society should not execute its fallen members, and that reason is a sociological one. Experience shows that in the great majority of cases men who commit crimes either are born criminals or have lived under such conditions that their environment promoted criminal instincts and even criminal traits. Had organized government done its duty towards such persons they would never have been criminals. Investigation shows that the majority of the inmates of the penitentiaries are illiterate. Many of them have no moral or religious training, and, of course, none of them are criminals from choice. They are " weak vessels," depraved degenerates, and, in many instances, monomaniacs. Yet we cry: " Hang them; hanging is too good for them!"
It is estimated by sociologists who have scientifically studied the question that 90 per cent of crimes committed would have been prevented had care, prudence and charity been exercised by the state and municipal governments. For example, the four gunmen of New York city sentenced to be hanged were victims of environment. They had been agents for gambling houses and houses of ill-lame, and divided their spoils with the officers of the law elected by the people of a great city. In that manner the agents of society educated them in crime, and yet the state says they must forfeit their blood to the state that trained them in vice. They were trained in the

under-world from infancy to commit crimes, till they became callous and did not scruple in taking life.
No state has the right to kill men when it contributes to their downfall. It owes them the duty to educate them and to throw nothing but moral influences around them, and when it fails to do this organized society is at fault. You may ask: What will we do with them? Why, do your duty towards them, by placing them in a prison, reformatory in its character; teach them morality, and, if necessary, give them mental training, and allow them the right to expiate their crimes and prepare for the hereafter. Make men out of them, and give them in most instances, if not in all, the hope that they will 'be rewarded if they will reform and become'worthy of again taking their places among their fellowmen. This young boy, Patrick Spain, went through the battle of Mons and was blown up by a German shell-a very severe case of shell shock. He was sent to a hospital, and as soon as he was able to be removed was moved to England. After spending considerable time in a hospital there, he was sent out to this country by some society, as they thpught his nerves "would have a better chance of being cured out in the prairies than in the city of London. It appears that this poor boy was brought up in the slums, knew nothing of education, moral or religious training. He was just a poor *little waif. He claims that he was sent info the house to clean his master's gun, and in doing so the gun accidentally went off and killed his employer's wife. His employer, having heard the shot, rushed towards the house with a gun in his hand. The boy claims that he did not know what he was doing at the time, that his nerves were so unstrung from the accident and from seeing the husband rush towards him with the gun in, his hand that he turned around and shot the husband. The whole thing was a matter of circumstantial evidence. The boy was only 16; surely we are not going to start hanging children in Canada. It is a long time since we have hanged a child and I hope that we shall not commence again in 1917. I have no doubt that few of the members of this House understand the nature of shell shook and the results which it causes. I do, a little. A grandson of mine was blown up by a shell at the battle of the Somme which took place several months ago, and he has been in an English hospital ever since and has not yet quite recovered. I am not sure but the hon. mem-
ber for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) met him; I think he did. My grandson's nerves are in a very shattered condition, and I question very much if he will ever be the same man again; and if this boy's nerves were in the same condition as my grandson's are in at the present time, he can hardly be accounted responsible for anything he did. It may be that the boy has killed or murdered. If my information is correct, he was tried, not for murdering the woman but for murdering the husband, but he was condemned to death for murdering the woman.

I hope Canada will not only save the boy but save our young nation from the everlasting disgrace of having hanged a child. I ask: Would society be any better protected now by sending this poor little boy into eternity than it would by sending him into a reformatory? Is there in this House to-day any man who will say he wants to hang a little boy of sixteen years of age? I do not think even the member for that constituency will say so. The hon. member was a little short the other evening and felt, like the Minister of Justice, that nothing but vengeance and justice would suit in this country, but on further consideration he did not, I think, feel quite so vengeful. This boy's father is still in the British Army fighting side by side with our young men at the front. The boy's sister is in a lunatic asylum in Ireland. My hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) shakes his head; but I am informed by the boy's lawyers, who, I understand, are a reputable firm, that such is the case. The family is an Irish one. The boy's father joined the British army and was sent over to England. The family moved to London and the little boy was brought up in the worst slums in that great

city. What could one expect? He went to the front as a bugler and his father is still in the army fighting for us. The poor little fellow sixteen years of age is now .a stranger in this country, and we say: Hang him. God forbid that this young nation will be so disgraced as to hang that boy. When this boy's comrades return from the front, they will ask the Minister of Justice: Where is our little comrade? I do not think they will be pleased when they find that their little bugler has been hanged. I am not speaking about law; I know very little about law, and what I do know has been very expensive.

For the benefit of our warrior bold from Peterborough (Mr. Burnham), I would like to read this editorial from the Peterborough Evening Review :
The right or one man to take the life of another in order to preserve his own has always heen recognized in human enactments and set forth in Divine law. The fact must be established that the man so acting in his own behalf had every reason to believe that his life was in danger before he resorted to extreme measures to protect it.
I am reading this for the benefit of my good friend who was very much taken with the question of self-defence:
This principle or legal maxim is one of the stock arguments of those who favor the retention of capital punishment. Society must be protected from the murderer, and to save its own existence must put all such out of the way. Surely society or the state is not threatened by the acts of a single individual, and is able to protect itself by adopting measures less harsh.
A grown man attacked toy a boy armed with a snowball or a bean-shooter may be annoyed, but it can hardly be claimed that his life is actually in danger. No matter what the inclination may be to play the role of Cain, adequate provocation is lacking. The boy can be suppressed and disposed of, made to see the error of his ways, reformed completely, perhaps, by some method short of shedding his blood. If his victim did take his life, the law would hardly uphold his procedure.
The illustration cited above represents, too, the individual homicide and the State. The latter is too big and powerful to set up the plea that it is in any real danger by reason of the acts of one lone offender. It is necessary as well as advisable for the State to protect itself, but surely this can be done without resorting to extreme measures. What right has the State, whose authority is delegated to it by the individual, to take human life, any more than the latter has to avenge himself of his adversaries in the same way?
There is certainly no warrant for such a line of conduct found in the teachings of the Naza-rene, upon Whose precepts all human legislation is supposed to be based.
A boy of sixteen, brought up in the slums of London, neglected, and surrounded with every form of vice, until he no doubt came to regard viciousness as the normal condition of humanity, was transplanted to new surroundings in Manitoba. The shifting of the scene was not sufficient to effect a change in a nature calloused by a youth spent in such environments as he had known. He committed a double murder under circumstances that at once stamped him as a moral and mental degenerate.
The boy is to toe hanged, despite his. years. Society takes the cheapest method of getting him out of the way. The powerful State confesses itself unable to handle a boy of sixteen short of breaking his neck. A grown man who acted as the State does in this case would not only toe laughed at but held to strict accountability.
One of the objections to capital punishment is that it tends to breed in the community a class of individuals only a shade less reprehensible than the murderer himself. The marvel is not so much that the State, coldblooded as it is, should decide to hang this boy, but that it should be able to find a man willing for a trifling monetary consideration to place the noose around the neck of the youth and spring the trap under his feet.
That is an editorial from, I think, the principal newspaper in my hon. friend's riding. If that boy's sister is in a lunatic asylum; if that boy was brought up in the slums of London with such an environment-if that is all true, is there a man in this House who would hang that child? I do not plead his innocence because he confesses frankly that he killed his boss. But surely no man will say that this was a cause of premeditated murder. It was committed on the spur of the moment, and many of the best lawyers think that it should have been a case of manslaughter and not of murder.
Hon. 0. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :	I do not purpose for a moment to
enter into any discussion of the hon. gentleman's motion. I think the House will realize how improper and impossible it would be for a member of this Government, which has imposed upon it the duty of advising His Excellency in the exercise of the prerogative of the Crown to grant leniency, to express any opinion on the matter in this Parliament, But realizing the very strong feeling pf the hon. gentleman upon this subject,. and not wishing to prevent his having the opportunity of making such plea as his heart might inspire on behalf of this young man, I did not when he moved this motion take exception on the ground

of its being put of order, nor do I now desire to make absolute affirmation upon that subject. But I do feel very strongly that I should submit to your judgment, Sir, the question of whether this motion is in order. I should like to point out that the exercise of clemency is the prerogative of the Crown, that His Excellency the Governor General exercises that prerogative under the powers conferred upon him by his commission. Under that commission he is required to act in capital cases upon the advice of his council, and in other cases upon the advice of one of his ministers, usually the Minister of Justice. Parliament does not appear to me to have any role t,o play in the matter, and from the practical point of view I think we can all realize what an unfortunate thing it would be if council, called upon to advise the Governor General say in this particular case, should find itself face to face with a vote of Parliament that this young man .ought to be hanged; because if there may 'be a vote that he should not hang, there may equally be a vote that he should. In what position to act impartially, to weigh the circumstances pro and con with the knowledge derived from a careful study of the entire evidence in the case, would the members of the council be,vif in advance they had the expression of the opinion of this Parliament (to which after all they are responsible), that the young man ought to hang? I think it is only necessary to point out that practical inconvenience, to strengthen the position that such a motion as is now made, inviting in advance of any action on the part of the Crown, an expression of opinion by Parliament as to what that action should be, is clearly out of order. I do not propose to go into the citation of authorities, because I did not come here prepared for that purpose, but the question is very fully discussed in Todd's Parliamentary Practice, and I think there is no conclusion that can be reached other than that this motion seeking to seize Parliament of this question at this stage is out of order.

Mr. JOHN H. SINCLAIR (Guysborough) moved:-
A return giving a list of all appointments made by the present Administration prior to the date of this order under the provisions of Section 21 of the Civil Service Act, 190S, giving the names in full, former Post Office addresses, occupations, ages, present employment, department in which employed, salaries at time of appointment, present yearly salaries and the respective dates of the Orders in Council by which they were appointed.
He said:	There is reason to suspect that
section 21 of the Civil Service Act has been used for purposes that were not intended at the time the Act was passed. The Civil Service Act, which was passed in 1908, was an attempt to supersede the old practice of appointing favourites to positions in the Civil Service; it was an honest attempt, I believe, to introduce a system of appointment by merit after competitive examination. It was found necessary, however, to make provision for exceptional cases in which it might be found inadvisable to demand that the candidate for appointment submit to examination. It was pointed out at the time that occasionally the Government might wish to appoint an eminent engineer or some other officer who would refuse to accept appointment if it were made conditional that he should undergo an examination. Consequently this section was put in the Act, giving the Government power with the consent of ' the Commission to override in a sense, by Order in Council, the Civil Service Commission. When a man of such character as I have referred to is required for the Civil Service, the Government may
appoint him by Order in Council, as I understand it. I asked the question a few days ago how many appointments had been made by the present Administration under this section and the Secretary of State (Mr. Patenaude) informed me that the number was 174.. I submit that there is reason to think that there have not been 174 appointments of genuine experts to the (fivil Service since 1911, and I am much inclined to suspect that many of these appointments were of men who were too old to be appointed under the Act, or were not well enough posted to pass the ordinary examination. Of course, I am not sure as to that, but the number of appointments strikes me as very large, and I think no hon. member will be of opinion that so many genuine appointments have been made under Section 21 within the last five years. However, I will reserve my criticisms until the report comes down. I would make special request of the Secretary of State not to delay the bringing down of the return. I find that there is a disposition this session to delay the production of papers. In my own experience and that of other hon. members, when a single question is asked the answer to which requires only a little work on the part of a clerk, the question is turned into an order for returns, pigeonholed and apparently forgotten, and it may ibe six months before the return is ready. I hope that will not be the case with this motion, as it is very important that we should stand by the intention of the Civil Service Act, and if there is an abuse in regard to section 21 the public and the House should know it.
I submit that it would 'be right for the Secretary of State to make a special case of this motion and to speed the production of the papers as much as possible.'

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, approval should be given to any measure proposed by the Government towards meeting the claims of the wives, families and dependents, of the men who lost their lives in the disaster to the Government Dredge Cape Breton, off Shad Rock, Guysbo-rough County, Nova Scotia, in the month of January last.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this resolution has reference to a very distressing disaster that occurred on the coast of Guysborough in January last. The Cape Breton was being towed from Lunenburg to Sydney. It was at a season of the year when, owing to the condition of the weather, the towing of such a helpless ship as this was extremely difficult. The result of this disaster was the loss of the lives of the members of the crew. Several of them belonged to the county I represent in this House; others were natives of other parts of the province of Nova Scotia. Those belonging to my county left wives and helpless families. Without desiring to introduce a harsh note into this discussion, I may say that the conditions under which the disaster took place imply that the Government is subject to more responsibility in regard to it than perhaps it otherwise would be. The moving of this dredge from Lunenburg to Sydney at that time was a proceeding that, with all deference to those who were responsible for it, should not have been undertaken. It has not been disclosed to my knowledge what urgent necessity there was for towing the dredge at that season of the year. It has been suggested that it was necessary to transport the Cape Breton on to Sydney for the purpose of having some repairs made to its machinery. I cannot understand why it was necessary to take the Cape Breton to Sydney at that season of the year. The repairs necessary to be made to the machinery, I am informed, could as well have been made in the town of Lunenburg, where there is a foundry and machine shop quite capable of supplying such machinery and repairs as were necessary. But, it the work could not have been done in Lunenburg it could have been done in the city of Halifax or in the town of Dartmouth. Another .circumstance that contributed, I think, to the disaster, or, at all events, which reduced the possibility of the escape of those who were on the dredge, was that the life-saving station at Whitehead was at that time out of commission. For some years a very efficient lifesaving station had been maintained at that point, which is a place very much exposed to the storms of the Atlantic, par-

ticularly during the winter season. For some reason of which I am not cognizant, the department of this Government having control over life-saving stations disbanded the life-saving crew, the boats were unfit to render service, and as a consequence of this, when the accident occurred to the Cape Breton, there was no life-saving apparatus available to assist in the rescue of these poor, unfortunate men. On account of these two circumstances, I suggest that the responsibility of the Government to make adequate allowance for the dependents of those who were lost in that disaster is greater than it would be under ordinary circumstances. In any con-ition the lose of the wage-earner is a very serious blow and entails very great privations in most cases upon those who are dependent upon him. At a time like this when the cost of living is so high and when it is very difficult" for those who are capable and competent to eg,rn their daily bread for themselves and their families to earn a sufficient amount for that purpose, what shall we say of the poor, unfortunate widow and helpless children who are faced with the necessity of earning for themselves a sufficient income to provide for the necessaries of life? What ever would have been the intention of the Government under ordinary conditions, I think the particular circumstances surrounding this disaster call for special treatment on the part of the Government. Some questions were asked in this House by my hon. friend representing the county of Guys-borough (Mr. Sinclair) as to what were the intentions of the Government in respect to this matter. The hon. acting Minister of Public Works (Mr. Reid) was good enough to reply that the matter was receiving the attention of the Government. I move this resolution for the purpose of impressing on the hon. acting Minister of Public Works and the other members of the Government that this case is one not requiring ordinary treatment and I would express the hope that when this question comes before them for their consideration they will deal ' with it in the broadest and most generous way that they possibly can. I shall not press consideration of it further upon the Government than to urge upon them that they will place a just measure of compensation and assistance, in the way of a gratuity, in the hands of those who are dependent upon themselves for their livelihood on account of the accident to which I have referred.

speechtext:
I should like to direct the attention of the acting Prime Minister to a matter which is of special importance on the coast of the Maritime provinces, that is, the scarcity of salt for the curing of fish. My hon. friend is aware that tonnage is now very scarce and as salt is a bulky material, compared with its value, it is difficult to procure tonnage to

deliver it on the coast where it is needed to prepare for the season s fishing. There is great scarcity of salt, and great danger that it will not he available to the fishermen. I have had letters and telegrams from different points on the coast stating that there is little or no sa.lt at Halifax, which was the place whence it was generally furnished, and that there is a prospect that it will be very scarce and that that scarcity will interfere with the industry during the present season. My hon. friend is no doubt aware that the fishermen, like the farmers, are being urged to increase production, and it is of the utmost importance that they should do so. The fishing on the coast of Europe has practically ceased. Prior to the war, at least 3 000 steam trawlers were carrying on fishing in the North Sea and in the adjoining waters, supplying most of Europe with fresh and salt fish. The war has changed all that, nearly all those trawlers being en<*a<md as mine-sweepers or as boats for the purpose of hunting the submarine, and little or no fishing is being carried on at the present time in Europe. It is therefore of the utmost importance that everything should be done to aid the Canadian fishermen, as they are at present supplying food to our soldiers at the front, large quantities of fresh fish having gone forward from Canada to France within the last number of months for that purpose. I do not know what steps the Prime Minister should take in the matter, but I have no doubt there are a good many transport ships coming across from the other side at the present time practically empty. Of course the ships are all loaded going east, but many of them come back in ballast, and there ought to be an opportunity of getting some of this salt taken over, possibly in some of the ships that are commandeered by the.Government. It is at all events worth while for my hon. friend to look into the matter, in order to see if anything can be done to relieve the situation, which, I believe, is very urgent, and likely to become more urgent if some steps are not taken.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in closing the debate, I will naturally be very brief, but as some very distinguished statesmen have taken exception to my Bill, I will take the opportunity of replying briefly to them. They all undertook to oppose my suggested amendment to the Criminal Code for the purpose of abolishing the death penalty and substituting life imprisonment for the different crimes contained in our statute books, for which the extreme penalty of death is prescribed. In doing so I would call the attention of the leader of the Opposition to some of his remarks as reported in Hansard, to which remarks I desire to take exception. Before doing so, however, I would like to say a few words in reply to the Solicitor General. I want to make it very plain that my view is that capital piinishment should not be abolished if hanging protects society. I take that ground at once. The first object that this Parliament should have is to protect society, and if it is necessary to hang our poor prodigals for the purpose of protecting society, then let us hang them. On

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS.

speechtext:
the other hand, if we can protect society equally well, or better, by life imprisonment, then let us have life imprisonment, but by all means let our first consideration be the protection of society. The Solicitor General took very strong grounds on that question the other evening.
Capital punishment is discriminatory. Because of its severity it is almost never inflicted upon a person of wealth or influence, and in general we hang only such as belong to the abjectly miserable portion of humanity. The long and short of the matter is that the death penalty is too severe to be inflicted upon the rich or the strong. It is one of the cruel inventions of caste-it is a class penalty, just as some of the laws governing it have been class laws. A penalty so severe as not to foe enforceable has a basic objection; it produces unrest to have a constant miscarriage of justice. A wealthy malefactor, an influential murderer, a powerful assassin cannot go free, in a community where paupers and friendless foreigners are hanged, without the people acquiring a contempt for the laws.
There is, regrettably, a disposition on the part of some of our most worthy citizens (yes, Christians) to bring passages of Scripture to the support of capital punishment. We have heard unto the point of weariness the quotation of the Old Testament of " an eye for an eye and- a tooth for a tooth. We do not hear so frequently, however, of Christ's own allusion to the Old Testament in the following words " Ye have heal'd it said in olden times, ' An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth,' but I say unto you, love your enemies and pray for them that despitefully use you." If any one, however adept in placing construction on the English language, is able, in the light of these words, to attribute even tacit support of the death penalty to the Saviour of mankind he will exceed all Pounds of mental agility within my comprehension. Again, we hear from those who would quote the Word in justification of legalized murder, the citing of that part of the sixth verse of the ninth chapter of Genesis, which reads as follows, Whosoever sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed."
Some of our best people try to be governed exclusively by what the Old Testament says. I revere and respect their opinions, but I must confess that I always prefer to have same endorsed by the New Testament. Now, it is within the memory of many that a large number of Christians in the Southern States quoted the Old
Testament in support of slavery. I also remember in my younger days Brigham Young quoting freely from the Old Testament in support of polygamy, but as neither slavery nor polygamy could be endorsed by the New Testament, they had to go, and for just the same reason will capital punishment have to go. I think that the environment in which we are living has a great influence on the community. Take, for example, was it not strange that Nero, " the monster of cruelty," should say during the first few years of his reign, when death warrants were presented him to sign, that he regretted that he had ever learned to write, so averse was he to shedding human blood. Later, when he became brutalized, he could sign them without pain, and put his own mother to death without remorse.
Now, Sir, the purest Being, the greatest Teacher, the holiest Judge who ever presided over the destinies of man, never wrote a sentence preserved in history excepting one when meditating upon capital punishment. He wrote with hie finger in the sand and then immediately said, as if an interpretation of what he wrote: "Let him who is without sin oast the first stone." The old law read:	"Let her be atoned to
death." As all men are sinners, this harsh and cruel law of death, written in the Old Testament, was reconstructed and repealed by the Saviour of man, and savage justice was tempered with the saving influence of the Master's mercy.
The next in order to attack the Bill was the right hon. leader of the Opposition. I am pleased to see the Government and the right hon. leader of the Opposition getting so close together. The Government has given the right hon. leader of the Opposition free wheat, and the leader of the Opposition, not to be outdone in politeness, has given the Government free hanging.

President Fallieres claims that if this were the case it would do away with all legalized homicide. He further says:
I will not ask any man to do that which I myself am unwilling to do. I will do no murder, even for the State.
President Fallieres therefore commuted all death penalties to life imprisonment. Where there was a reasonable doubt about a man's guilt he pardoned him. He also says:
France must learn to take care of her criminals without killing them. It is a poor use to make of a man to take his life. It is an acknowledgment of our inefficiency. Then, a life sentence should hold out to a man the promise that a number of years of good behaviour and useful work will make him free. Penology must be made a science to the end that when we imprison a man we do it for his own good, with the intention of turning out a better man than we took in. Just as long as the State sets an example of killing its enemies, they must expect that individuals will occasionally kill theirs.
The right hon. leader of the Opposition says:

Whether or not the penalty of death is a deterrent is a much mooted question. Education has more to do with the prevention of crime than even the deterrent effect of the punishment, and in this country it can happily be said that cases of murder are very few, in fact, amongst the native population; they are becoming less and less frequent.
With that statement I quite agree. The right hon. leader of the Opposition goes on:
All the cases which have taken place recently have been amongst a class of foreigners who come from a country In which the crime of murder is a daily custom. Without being invidious, I believe that many crimes of that nature have been committed by Italians w-ho came from the South of Italy, where It is the ____imnnD ii.iV.it nf every man to carry a stiletto.
With -this latter statement I can hardly agree. The only execution in the province of Quebec during 1916 was that of Paul dit-Lepine Renaud, and judging by the name, he could have hardly been an Italian.
The name of the young lad 10 p.m. lying under sentence of death in Winnipeg is Patrick Spain; that does not sound like an Italian either. So I think the contention of the right hon. leader of the Opposition that all the murders in Canada are committed by men who come from the south of Italy is wrong. I have no doubt the right hon. gentleman is aware that Italy abolished capital punishment years ago. Further on he said:
What is the most effective law? Shall we continue the law which we have had on the Statute Book ever since the country has been a country, and which is still a law among the most civilized nations of the earth? Or shall we be carried away by a feeling of humanity which is most commendable and most honourable?
Now, Sir, I think I- have proved to the right hon. gentleman that it is not the foreign element in Canada who are committing all the murders. With regard to the claim that capital punishment is right because it has been on the statute book ever since this country has been a country, and because it is still the law among the most civilized nations of the earth. I remember welil the time when the right hon. gentleman refused to follow custom, and claimed that this young nation was now grown up and should make the laws that were considered most necessary for our Dominion. Custom never did make right. With regard to his claim that this is still the law among the most civilized nations of the earth, I must also join issue with him. He claims that it is the most civilized nations of the world that retain capital punishment. On the contrary, the nations that have abolished capital punishment are not the

heathen or uncivilized nations, but just the reverse. According to the right hon. leader of the Opposition China is one of the most civilized nations of the world. China, Turkey, Japan, 'Germany and Austria-Hungary all have capital punishment. The other three nations that retain capital punishment are England, France and Spain. I am prepared to say that these are civilized nations, but they are the only civilized nations that retain capital punishment. Now, I desire to place opposite to these the names of the anti-hanging countries-I suppose, the right hon. gentleman would call them "the uncivilized nations." They are: Russia-surely, not an uncivilized country- Italy, Holland, Belgium, Norway, Portugal, Haiti, Switzerland and the United States (in part). I cannot understand the statement made by the right hon. gentleman. He quotes the "civilized nations" as the excuse for retaining capital punishment, and the greatest nation that retains it is China. If he holds China to be one of the civilized Christian nations of the world, of course he is quite entitled to his opinion.
I hold that the death penalty is the most atrocious form of bookkeeping in existence. The only way we can balance a debit is by a credit; you can only balance a negative by a positive; the only way to balance evil is by good. It is a most ridiculous thing to have a death entered on one side of the ledger, and then expect to balance it by turning'to the other side and writing down another death. That is the style of bookkeeping of the Minister of Justice, so far as this branch of his business is concerned. I would like to see capital punishment abolished for the sake of the innocent men who have been executed, and there have been a numbed of them. I wish to quote from a letter written by the man who, I suppose, is the greatest authority on prison reform on this side of the water, if not in the -world-Thomas Mott Osborne, of Sing Sing fame. He says:
As warden of Sing Sing I executed forty men, and I am convinced that four of them were innocent. One was a hoy of 20 years of age, and I knew he was innocent of the crime for which . he was condemned, because I know who committed the crime. But the ethics of the underworld are that one must never 'squeal on a paly This hoy lied, evaded, faced his trial, was condemned, and afterwards went to his death, just because he would not 'squeal on a pal.' Was not that boy worth saving?
Is there any man in this House who will say that it was not worth while to try to
save such a boy? Innocent of the crime, he would not go back on his pal, but kept his course even though it led to the electric chair. I say to the Minister of Justice that if boys of that kind are not worth saving, then life is not worth, living.
Now I desire to say a few words in answer to the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). Hon. members will recollect that he quoted the Old Testament very freely. But the Old Testament is a record of the Jewish race, and it is difficult to see how it can be made the standard for Christians, especially when the Master enjoins His followers to forsake the old commands and gave them the new ones instead. He did not preach revenge but exhorted His followers to love their enemies. It must be recalled that the ancient prophets also looked to the time when swords would be beaten into ploughshares, and spears into pruning-hooks.
The great promised Messiah was to be a Prince of Peace; not one who took life but one who reformed it. There are very few students of the New Testament who attempt the tremendous task of defending capital punishment on its authority, for its teaching is mercy, long suffering, kindness, forgiveness, and these are not compatible with breaking a man's neck. The Master, as we are told in the 12th chapter of John,
* commutes the sentence of stoning to death, which the Jewish law imposed upon the adulterous woman, to the sentence "go and sin no more," bidding her accuser who was without sin to cast the first stone.
Life sentence is practical. I am not asking for a substitute for capital punishment which has not been tried. The states and nations that have actually substituted life imprisonment for capital punishment bear the testimony that it works well. Governor Washburn, of Wisconsin, said in 1873:
It is twenty years since we have abolished capital punishment and no state can show greater freedom from homicidal crimes... . With a population embracing almost every nationality, statistics show that crime instead of increasing with the growth, has actually diminished.
Senator Jessup, of Iowa, says:
Murder in the first degree has not increased but has for four years decreased,
And he gives figures to prove the truth of his assertion, and adds the significant expression-"there is more lynch law where the scaffold is retained."

Under life sentences juries convict and that speedily. The Chief Justice of Rhode Island says:
My observation fully justifies me in saying that conviction is far more certain now in proper cases than when the death penalty was in vogue.
Chief Justice Denman says:
Extreme severity has operated more as a pre-ventitive to prosecutions than a preventitive to crime.
Judges often find their juries returning and asking, ''Can we find a verdict of manslaughter"? and when the judges say. "No you cannot," they return with a verdict, "Not guilty."
Capital Punishment Is Not Effective-Capital punishment is no punishment to the .criminal, it is a greater punishment to the innocent members of his family. It is no punishment to break a man's neck. Juries hesitate to convict when they know a man is going to be hanged, and as a consequence only one in seventy-three murderers brought to trial in United States is convicted on first degree murder.
Capital punishment does not deter from crime. It is a fact which can be demonstrated by .statistics that where capital punishment flourishes murder likewise flourishes. Crime was on the increase in England until the two hundred odd capital offenses were reduced to two, and the same promptness in convictions in England without the death penalty would prove more efficacious in preserving law and order.
Men who witness and who read of capital punishment become vindictive. The chaplain of Newgate prison says that he "never knew a condemned criminal that had not been at an execution." (Westminster Review, '81: 162). Rev. J. Roberts of Bristol says that out of 180 persons whom he visited after the sentence of death, 164 had attended a public hanging. Those who see the brutality of the death chamber are only made more brutal. Capital punishment often leads to such public sympathy that the hands of justice are thwarted.
Qapital punishment is not moral-The state sets a wrong example to its citizens by punishing its offenders with death. Capital punishment diminishes the sacredness with which we should regard life. It destroys the moral sense of the public. It arouses the worst passions in man. During public executions in England, the gallows were scenes of wild debauch, the public eating, drinking, cheering and railing at the victim. Suicides or deaths of an ex-
citing nature are likely to be followed by others of like nature
There are many who question the right of one man to take another man's life except in self-defense when other means of defense fail. Wendel Phillips says:
The theory of government, as Is universally held, is that a government is a social compact, a voluntary association of individuals, therefor, as an individual has no right to take hisown life, he cannot confer on the government the right to take it.
Capital punishment is not justice, for often it endangers the lives of the wrong persons. Many of our criminals are murderers toy circumstances; men of wealth aTe rarely hanged, and often innocent people have been unjustly deprived of their life.
The judgments of judges and juries are not always infallible. The great Lafayette said:	'	.
I shall personally demand the abolishment of punishment by death until X have the infallibility of human judgment demonstrated to me.
There are a few who defend capital punishment from the authority of the Old Testament, but it must be remembered that the Lord set a mark on Cain, the first murderer,' and let him go. Moses taught a life for a life.
I must say a few word^ in reply to my hon. friend from Montcalm (Mr. Lafor-tune). The most powerful case cited by Mr. McConnico was the Durand case, in California. I am not sure whether I have mentioned this Durand case on previous occasions to the Minister of Justice. It was a case in which a young man was hanged for the murder of a young woman. They were both members of a Methodist church, both teachers in the same Sunday school, both singers in the same choir. One day the young lady disappeared. Suspicion immediately fell on the young man. He was arrested, tried and sentenced to death. He delivered a little, short speech-I remember the case well-just before he was sent into eternity. He said to the people there: I am not guilty of this crime; I am going to be hanged for a crime that I did not commit; and I say it before God and man. He lifted his eyes to heaven, and asked the Lord to forgive those who had sworn him to death. Sir, less than twelve months after that young man was sentenced to eternity, the minister of that congregation took sick and confessed that he was the man who had killed that girl. Well, the young man had gone into eternity. Now, I appeal to you, Mr. Speaker, I appeal to the Minister of Justice, if life imprisonment will serve society just as well, if life imprisonment will protect society as well as the death penalty, then why not let us make the experiment?
I must say a few words in reply to my good friend the member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury). I accused him this afternoon of being one who out-Heroded Herod. But I take that back; I should not have said that. I want to say to him, however, that the state does not kill people merely because they are worthless, and to be rid of them. Insane asylums are built at great expense for the incurable, upon whom relatives cannot bear to look, who personally might be better off dead. The state tenderly cares

for all such cases. This is done because the example of kindness and humanity to the unfortunate is of an inestimable benefit to society. It is not possible to imagine the effect society would feel if we were to destroy 'all imbeciles and the incurably insane. What a horrible example would be set for the people of the state to follow. No calculation could be made of the injury to the morals of the state by countenancing such conduct. One of the greatest advantages to the state from the preservation and tender care and treatment of the hopeless insane is this example of humane treatment and of tender consideration of a human life, however useless and pitiable it may seem. Our citizens are taught to be kind and gentle to the unfortunate by this example of the state. May I ask the people of Canada if they believe any boy-any mother's son, black or white, however depraved-should be hanged, killed just to get rid of him? Can we afford to do it?
Chief Baron Kelly says that from 1802 to 1840 he traced twenty-two men who were wrongly convicted of murder in England, seven of whom were hanged. Mackintosh says that in the same country, taking a long period of time, one innocent man is hanged in every three years.
It may be safely asserted that the thousands who were put to death, at the stake and otherwise, for witchcraft, were not guilty of the crime with which they were charged. Again, there is no way of ascertaining to a certainty the guilt of any one charged with murder. Felonious intent is the essence of crime. The jury must determine, then, in each instance the state of mind of the accused. In many cases this is a difficult task, and in not a few the verdict is a mere guess. A confession of guilt, if voluntary, would seem to be a strong evidence, but by way of illustrating a general rule, it will be remembered that a number of men confessed to the murder of Nathan in New York city, all of whom were innocent. In some cases of acknowledged murder the supposed victim has turned out to be still alive, and in at least one instance interrupted the trial.
Whatever may be the testimony of a witness, it cannot be certain to a demonstration, in most cases, that he is not committing perjury, or is not mistaken.
Of course I am aware that many will disagree with me, for I have never been' able to get everybody to see my way and be right in their view, but I am sure that, as men grow more civilized, capital punish-

ment grows less popular, and wholesale murder, in the shape of war, is regarded as the last resort by the civilized nations of the earth, and the time will come when human life will be rightly valued and war shall be no more. If this is not to be the case, Christianity will have proved a failure, to become an effete religion, cast by intelligent humanity upon the religious scrap pile of the ages.
Is it not time to put aside the unwarranted penalty of capital punishment and adopt the more humane and effective punishment by life imprisonment, put beyond the reach of one-man pardon? The capital punishment experiment has proved a failure, so far as its being a remedy for crime is concerned.
No matter how great any man's respect for the Old Testament may be, the most that he can say for the ceremonial and criminal law of the Hebrews is that it was adapted to men in a very crude condition, who were making their first advances in the rudiments of moral and religious truths; that it taught them only as much as they were prepared to receive, with a promise of something better to come after. The clergy admit that the ceremonial law of the Jews is no longer binding. They insist that God's covenant with Noah, in which occurs the verse, "Whoso sheddeth man's blood by man shall his blood be shed," is binding for all time and upon all nations. They do not understand that it is repealed, both in the language and the spirit of the New Testament. If they believe as firmly as they pretend that killing the murderer is-pleasing to God and a duty sacredly enjoined upon man, they should act as executioners: they certainly should not hesitate to pull the string or cut the rope that sends the soul of a murderer to the answering bar of God.

There is a wonderful growth of interest in the question of capital punishment. Students of criminology everywhere are discussing this theme. There are four hundred reform societies in the world pleading, as I do now, to spare human life whenever it is possible. A rising tide of humanitarianism is sweeping all the barbarities of the past before it, and as this matter is to be put before the voters of Canada, it is vitally important that we consider it at this time. In the hope that further study of the matter will be stimulated, I am presenting what is merely an outline of this great problem, and giving a few of the reasons why capital punishment should be abolished in Canada.
The abolition of capital punishment is the inevitable trend of history. While capital punishment may have been necessary in early history, there being no adequate prisons to hold extreme offenders of the common law, states and commonwealths are now rapidly abolishing it. During the last one hundred years there has been a wonderful decrease in the number of crimes punishable by death, because the death penalty was found to be ineffectual in preventing crime. A century ago England imposed the death penalty for two hundred and some odd transgressions of the civil law, but these have been reduced to two- murder and treason. Lord Eldon and Lord Ellenborough predicted chaos if men should not be hanged for petty larceny.
Holland abolished capital punishment in 1870. The statistics show nineteen murders from 1861 to 1870, while from 1870 to 1879 there were only seventeen murders, with an increase of population.
Finland has had no executions since 1824. A judge of the Court of Appeals writes: "The security of persons or property has not been in the least diminished by the abolition of capital punishment."
Switzerland abolished capital punishment in 1874. Later three cantons voted to sustain the death penalty in their jurisdiction. The remaining nineteen still thrive without the death penalty, and murder has not increased. .
Other countries and states which have abolished the death penalty are Portugal, Holland, Italy, Norway, Rumania, Tuscany, Costa Rica, Brazil, Ecuador, Guatemala and Venezuela. Denmark has had no hanging since 1890. Belgium none since 1863. Russia has recently abolished it entirely, and in none of these countries has crime increased.
